newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In: Checking the pulse of the Web.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In: Checking the pulse of the Web.

text.p: Remember the dire, but conflicting predictions of how the World Wide Web was going to collapse? At one point it was doomed to failure because huge demand was going overload communications and cause a general failure.

Almost in tandem, others were forecasting that people were finally getting bored with this fad called the Net and were soon going to stop visiting the fancy Web sites companies had dropped millions of dollars on.
To our collected relief, the Web is not dead. In fact, judging by the hundreds of millions of dollars flowing into the medium, it doesn't even appear to be on its last legs.

"Has the Net Finally Reached the Wall?" asked a headline from an August, 1996 Business Week article. At the start of this year, the Wall Street Journal weighed in with a much-discussed front-page story outlining all the big failures of some of the prominent Web sites and companies.

Since the articles were written, there have been many more failures, big and small, on the Net. The bankruptcy last month of Nets Inc., the Internet commerce outfit headed by former Lotus Developments Chief Executive Jim Manzi, was certainly another sign for some that the Internet sky was falling after all.

Yet somehow, the Web is still with us in mid-1997 and some would say the pulse is quickening, not fading. Perhaps it's like any gold rush, in that there are many big winners and many In the Klondike of the 1990s it is clear money is out there on the Internet, and many would say we are still only in the early stages of tapping the rich veins of cyber minerals.

Media consultants Cowles/Simba released a study last week predicting Internet advertising revenues would grow rapidly in the coming year. It predicts that by 2000, revenues could zoom to $2.46 billion from an estimated $446.2 million in 1997.

Web ad revenues still look pint-sized compared with the total $175 billion advertising industry, but what people should look at is the growth in the money flowing into Internet publishing. If the Cowles/Simba projections for 2000 prove correct, ad revenues would have jumped 941.2 percent over the $236.4 million realized in 1996.

"Factors leading to this growth include the proliferation of inexpensive Web access; the development of accurate and timely audience measurement services; increases in user sessions and page views/impressions; and the growing rate of moderate and frequent Web users," the report said.

After its research and contacts with the company's 15,000 worldwide clients, the group believes they are being realistic in their forecasts and also feel the numbers could improve even more if advertisers could get an accurate measurement on just how many surfers are out there.

"Until standardized hard data about the size and demographic composition of the Web audience become routinely available, Web ad expenditures will continue to pale in comparison to mass-market print and broadcast media," Cowles/Simba analyst Matthew Kinsman told Reuters.

Cowles/Simba gamely predict that "user sessions" on the Web will grow to 3.52 billion by 2000 from 1.85 billion sessions in 1997. This kind of activity will mean surfers will view a staggering 24.62 billion Web pages in 2000, up from 14.87 billion pages in 1997.
That is a lot of viewing and clicking by any measurement. Obviously, advertisers need to find out where people are surfing to now and where they will be going in the future.
But any way you sift through those figures, it is apparent that Web users will not be surfing the River Styx any time soon.
